n: The first of five visions: God forms a swarm of locusts just as the second crop begins to sprout, after the king had taken his share. Losing this crop would mean starvation.

f.g: The first cutting of hay, apparently taken as a royal tax.

n: As the locusts finish eating, Amos pleads, “Lord, forgive! How can Jacob survive? He is so small.” The prophet intercedes for the very people he warns.

f.g: The people of Israel, called by their ancestor’s name.

n: The Lord relents: “It will not happen.” Prayer matters; a prophet’s plea changed what came next.

f.g: Relented, changed course — not that God had sinned.

n: Second vision: the Lord calls for a judgment by fire so fierce it dries up the great deep beneath the earth and starts consuming the land.

f.g: Or “the land” — the allotted portion of farmland.

n: Again Amos begs God to stop, using the same plea: Israel is too small to survive this.
Again the Lord relents. Twice mercy wins — but the next visions show patience has limits.
Third vision: the Lord stands beside a wall built true to a plumb line, holding a plumb line in His hand.

f.g: A string with a weight, used by builders to check whether a wall is perfectly vertical.

n: God will measure Israel against His standard. Like a crooked wall, they will be found out of line, and He will no longer overlook it. This time Amos doesn’t intercede.
Israel’s shrines will be destroyed, and the royal house of Jeroboam will fall by the sword. Jeroboam II’s son Zechariah was assassinated after only six months.

f.g: Here a poetic name for Israel.

n: Amaziah, the priest at the royal shrine of Bethel, reports Amos to the king as a traitor. Authorities often call God’s messengers troublemakers.

f.g: Not the same as King Amaziah of Judah.

n: Amaziah twists Amos’s words slightly; Amos had spoken against Jeroboam’s house, but the message of exile was accurate.

f.w: Jeroboam shall die by the sword
f.g: Amos actually said the sword would come against “the house of Jeroboam” (v. 9).

n: Amaziah sneers, “Go home to Judah, seer, and make your living prophesying there.” He assumes Amos preaches for pay.
“Don’t prophesy at Bethel; this is the king’s sanctuary.” Amaziah treats the shrine as belonging to the king, not to God.

f.g: The royal sanctuary — a state temple.

n: Amos answers: “I was not a professional prophet or trained in a guild. I was a herdsman and tended sycamore figs.” His authority came from God’s call, not credentials.

f.g: A member of a prophetic school or guild (“sons of the prophets”), as in 2 Kings 2:3.
The sycamore fig had to be nicked to ripen; it was poor man’s fruit.

n: “The Lord took me from following the flock and said, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’” Like David, Amos was called from shepherding.

f.w: the LORD took me as I followed the flock

n: Amos turns the tables on Amaziah: you tell me not to preach against Israel? Then hear what God says about you.

f.g: Don’t let your words drip — don’t preach.

n: Amaziah’s family will suffer the horrors of conquest, his land will be divided among others, and he himself will die in exile in a pagan land. Israel will surely go into captivity.

f.g: Measured out with a surveyor’s cord and given to new owners.
